- When sentiment is consistently negative (especially > 3 consecutive negative values), model tends to overcorrect downward — reduce forecasted drop magnitude.
- After a sharp price spike, model often overshoots downward in the next few days — cap the immediate drop to avoid overcorrection.
- If recent history shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3+ consecutive price declines), model tends to over-predict further decline — adjust downward bias by 5–10% for next 3–5 days.
- When sentiment is neutral or slightly positive, model often underestimates upward momentum — increase forecast slightly above recent mean.
- Model frequently underestimates true price volatility in early horizon (e.g., 1–3 days ahead) — add 1–2% buffer for volatility spikes.
- If sentiment turns positive after a negative streak, model often fails to react — delay upward adjustment until sentiment stabilizes or confirms trend.
- For 30-day forecasts, model tends to overestimate downward drift in bearish sentiment — apply upward bias of 2–5% if sentiment is negative or neutral.
- If sentiment is volatile (rapid swings), model often misreads direction — use 3-day moving average of sentiment to smooth forecast direction.
